newsitem.title: POLAND: Gdansk shipyard workers hurl contempt at banks.
newsitem.headline: Gdansk shipyard workers hurl contempt at banks.

text.p: Workers yelling "Thieves, Thieves" flung coins -- and abuse -- on Monday at banks that have refused credit to the failing Gdansk shipyard, while the Solidarity union planned nationwide protests.

About 1,500 employees marched on Bank Gdanski's head office in the Baltic port city and a branch of Pekao, which have both rejected pleas from the bankrupt yard for a lifeline $100 million credit to build five ships for a German owner.
They also resumed last week's tactic of blocking the city's most vital crossroads with burning tyres for one hour, plunging traffic into chaos.

Meanwhile a special committee of Solidarity, which arose at the yard in 1980 as the Soviet bloc's first free trade union, was due on Monday to decide details of a country-wide campaign against the impending liquidation of the enterprise.
"As early as this week protests may start in other enterprises throughout the country in defence of the Gdansk shipyard," Solidarity chief Marian Krzaklewski told Reuters.

The latest outcry has erupted since the receiver of the 60-percent state-owned yard, which has been bankrupt since August last year, this month announced he would begin to lay off the remaining 3,800 employees staff and sell off assets.

The pro-Catholic, rightist union accuses the government led by former communists of letting the yard perish out of malice, because it was a bastion of the pre-1989 fight against communism and remains an opposition stronghold.

The nationwide action may be too late to save the yard in its current shape, although Solidarity is also trying to raise millions of dollars to rescue it by selling coupons to the public, possibly at churches, rail stations and post offices.

But its agony is a powerful symbol for rallying the rightist opposition grouped in the Solidarity Election Action (AWS), an alliance of rightist parties the union has formed to challenge the left in general elections due around September.
Pope John Paul ll underlined its meaning for those Poles for whom Catholicism and the democracy struggle were linked.

"I want to tell you that, just as I was with you in heart and prayer when you fought for freedom, so I am now with you and your families in this struggle for survival," the Pontiff said in Polish after his regular Sunday angelus address.
Realising the yard's power as a symbol, politicians of various hues are now urging its rescue -- notably Waldemar Pawlak, head of the co-ruling Polish Peasant Party (PSL).

The Peasants, rooted in the communist era, aim to distinguish themselves from their larger ex-communist partner the Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) and Pawlak has said that banks might have offered loans if the SLD had urged them to.

The head of the yard's Solidarity branch, Jerzy Borowczak, dismissed as an empty pre-election stunt a weekend offer by the SLD's Gdansk provincial governor to take over the assets of the yard and restructure them, if the government assumed its debts.
During Monday's protest Borowczak also took a swipe at other parties belatedly rushing in with verbal support.
"I begin to suspect that other groupings speaking out about the yard are also paying more heed to electoral campaign goals than to our fate," he said during Monday's protest.

The SLD's Economy Minister Wieslaw Kaczmarek, who argues that the yard's problems are the result of past mismanagement and the banks merely did their sums and refused credit for sound independent reasons, mocked Pawlak's intervention.
"This is a (communist) party mentality...from the 1970s and 1980s which said that a directive from some party hack could mobilise bank credit," Kaczmarek told private Radio Zet.
Nevertheless, he said he still believed shipbuilding of some kind could continue at the site.
